newsitem.title: HONG KONG: WEEK AHEAD-Hong Kong stocks face tough time.
newsitem.headline: WEEK AHEAD-Hong Kong stocks face tough time.

text.p: A tough week lies ahead for Hong Kong stocks, with worries about higher interest rates and plummeting Japanese shares adding to concerns that imminent government curbs on property prices are likely, analysts said.

"I think investors are quite concerned about three major factors: one is the rising U.S. long bond yield, the other is the Nikkei's freefall and the third item is the impending government crackdown on property speculators," said Alex Tang, head of research at Yamaichi International.
The Hang Seng index slipped 6.61 points or 0.05 percent on Friday to close at 13,191.50. Over the week, the blue chip index lost 31.29 points or 0.24 percent.

Despite a new record high in the Dow industrials on Friday, analysts said Hong Kong stocks could head lower after a strong U.S. December jobs report heightened fears that the U.S. Federal Reserve could raise interest rates soon.
The U.S. Labour Department said on Friday that non-farm payrolls rose by 262,000 in December, more than the 192,000 forecast by Wall Street economists.

The Dow industrials shrugged off the report, jumping 78.00 points to 6,703.67, but the U.S. long bond slid 1-6/32 to yield 6.85 percent. Traders said the report had given equity markets a boost by suggesting fourth quarter earnings would be good.
Hong Kong stocks in London tumbled with the Hang Seng London Reference index shedding 210.07 points to 12,981.43.
"Even though the Dow Jones finally gained 78 points, I think an imminent interest rate hike will overshadow the stock market," said Patrick Chia, research director at China Everbright Research.
Tang said the U.S. Federal Reserve could raise interest rates some time this quarter. The Federal Open Market Committee next meets on February 4 and 5.

Analysts said interest-rate sensitive property counters were likely to be pressured the most with the added possibility of Hong Kong government measures to reign in escalating property prices causing further weakness. Speculation has been mounting that the government could act as early as this week.
Analysts said investors would be closely watching Wednesday's government land auction -- the first this year -- for clues about the property market's future direction.

A plot situated on the south side of Hong Kong island in Repulse Bay is likely to be the main focus of the auction since it has been earmarked for luxury residential use. Experts say speculation has been rampant in that end of the market.
Analysts said a continued decline in Japanese share prices could also hurt sentiment in Hong Kong. The Nikkei average of 225 shares plummeted 4.26 percent to 17,303.65 on Friday.
"Following the sharp fall in Japanese stocks, I think sentiment towards Hong Kong stocks may now become more cautious. The Hong Kong market is unlikely to make much headway next week," said Tang.
He said the index was likely to start on a weak note on Monday "and most likely test the immediate support level at 13,000 points".

Sunny Chan, senior research manager at Seapower Securities, said the Hang Seng should find firm support at 13,000 points, but harsh government measures in the property market could bring the index down to 12,800 points.
"It could go back above 13,000 by the end of the week," added Tang. "I think anything below 13,000 is a bargain."

Blue chip Great Eagle Holdings Ltd is due to release its final results on Wednesday. Shares in Wah Lee Resources Holdings Ltd, an air-conditioning systems, audio visual and photographic products distributor, are due to begin trading on Friday.
